paras: The false report of a lynching at Tompkinsville, Kentucky, was a one-sentence wire item of early January 1888 stating that five 'bond robbers and incendiaries' had been taken from the Tompkinsville jail by a mob and lynched. Dispatches from Glasgow and Louisville in the same days reported instead that the five men accused of robbing and burning Tompkinsville had come before the Monroe Circuit Court, where three were sentenced to the penitentiary and two were discharged.

According to a Louisville dispatch of January 5, 1888, a gang had committed a burglary of some $20,000 at Tompkinsville about two months earlier and had set fire to the town 'in the hope of escaping in the confusion.' Five men were arrested at Knoxville and carried to Tompkinsville to answer charges of robbery and arson.

A Glasgow dispatch reported that the Monroe Circuit Court convened at Tompkinsville on a Monday and that the grand jury returned three indictments the next day against each of two brothers named Clark, alias Reeves, and a man named Mallard. The three pleaded guilty to burglary and not guilty to burning the court house, and a jury returned a guilty verdict after only a few minutes. The Savannah Morning News put the total sentence at thirty years each, while the Louisville wire and later notices gave thirty-one years and one roundup gave twenty.

The other two prisoners, W. H. Reeves and S. M. Reeves, alias Hudson, were expected to be charged as accessories, but the grand jury ignored the charges and the court discharged them. A Glasgow special to the Louisville Courier-Journal described the pair arriving in Glasgow on the evening of January 7, drunk and 'very abusive of the newspapers.'

The lynching claim ran as an unheaded sentence in boilerplate news columns, in the Abbeville Press and Banner's 'Later News' on January 4 and in 'South and West' columns in Kingwood, West Virginia, and Edenton, North Carolina, on January 5 and 6. It gave no date, names or source, and no follow-up repeating it was found.
The trial itself was carried under the headline 'Kentucky Desperadoes' in Savannah and as news of 'the notorious Reeves gang' in Mississippi, and none of these court reports mentioned a mob.

Only the roundup sentence says the five prisoners were lynched, while dated dispatches from Glasgow and Louisville name the same men and report their sentences or release. Because the court reports are local, dated and specific, they are the stronger evidence, and the lynching item appears to have been a garbled version of the Tompkinsville case.

reader.title: False report of a lynching at Tompkinsville, Kentucky (1888)
bases: A wire roundup item reported five prisoners lynched at Tompkinsville (A1), but dated dispatches from Glasgow and Louisville show the five men accused of the Tompkinsville burglary and arson were tried, three sentenced and two discharged in the same days (A2, A4, A6), so the item is a false or garbled lynching report rather than an episode of mob violence.

The only report of a lynching is an undated, unsourced roundup sentence (A1, reprinted A3, A5); dated court dispatches report that three of the five prisoners were convicted and sentenced on or about Jan. 4 and the other two discharged on Jan. 7 (A2, A4, A6), which no lynching of all five could allow.
One wire sentence reports five prisoners lynched (A1, A3, A5), while several independent dispatches and roundups report the same men tried, sentenced or released (A2, A4, A6, A7, A8).

framing.detail: The lynching item was one unheaded sentence among unrelated wire items in 'LATER NEWS' and 'South and West' columns.
The court news called the prisoners 'Kentucky Desperadoes', 'a Bad Gang' and 'the notorious Reeves gang' and reported the sentences without mention of any mob.
